# Molluscum contagiosum

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Pediatrics > Pediatric dermatology > Molluscum contagiosum*

[Original Article Link](/library/-40DNT)

---

## Summary

Molluscum contagiosum is a common <u>skin infection</u> caused by the <u>molluscum contagiosum virus</u> and typically manifests on the trunk, face, and genitalia. Molluscum contagiosum is most common in childhood and early <u>adolescence</u> and is usually transmitted in this age group via <u>skin</u> contact and <u>autoinoculation</u>. In adults, it is often sexually transmitted. Lesions typically manifest as smooth, dome-shaped <u>papules</u> with central <u>umbilication</u>, localized on the trunk and face in children and lower abdomen and groin in adults. Molluscum contagiosum is usually <u>self-limiting</u> and resolves spontaneously within 1 year. Treatment may be indicated for symptomatic control, cosmesis, <u>infection control</u>, and in <u>immunosuppressed</u> individuals with widespread, persistent lesions. <u>Cryotherapy</u>, <u>curettage</u>, and topical <u>cantharidin</u> are the preferred treatment options. <u>Isolation precautions</u> are usually not indicated as the risk of transmission is typically low.

---

## Epidemiology

* Sex: <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u>

* Age: most common in childhood (peak <u>incidence</u> < 5 years of age) and early <u>adolescence</u>

* <u>Prevalence</u>

* More common in warm and humid climates or areas with poor hygiene

* More common in <u>immunocompromised individuals</u>; up to 20% of <u>HIV</u>-positive patients have symptomatic infection. [[1]](/library/8SdOYp0)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

* <u>Pathogen</u>: molluscum contagiosum virus (a <u>DNA</u> <u>poxvirus</u>)

* Transmission [[2]](/library/Bedza60)

* Direct <u>skin</u> contact (e.g., through contact sports, sexual contact)

* <u>Autoinoculation</u> (from scratching, shaving, or touching)

* <u>Fomites</u> (e.g., on bath sponges or towels)

* <u>Vertical transmission</u>

* <u>Incubation period</u>: typically 2–7 weeks  [[1]](/library/8SdOYp0)[[2]](/library/Bedza60)

---

## Clinical features

* Appearance [[2]](/library/Bedza60)

* Solitary or multiple nontender, <u>skin</u>-colored, pearly, dome-shaped <u>papules</u> with central <u>umbilication</u>

* Usually 2–5 mm in diameter

* Possible perilesional pruritic <u>eczematous</u> reaction (<u>molluscum dermatitis</u>) [[1]](/library/8SdOYp0)[[2]](/library/Bedza60)

* Typical distribution [[1]](/library/8SdOYp0)[[2]](/library/Bedza60)

* In children: face, trunk, and extremities

* In adults or in sexually transmitted cases: lower abdomen, groin, genitalia, and <u>proximal</u> thighs





> [!TIP]
> Lesions are often widespread, large, and persistent in <u>immunocompromised</u> patients and those with <u>atopic dermatitis</u>. [[2]](/library/Bedza60)[[3]](/library/tSdXYp0)[[4]](/library/73d4Pp0)

---

## Diagnosis

* Diagnosis is primarily clinical; <u>dermoscopy</u> can aid visualization.  [[1]](/library/8SdOYp0)[[2]](/library/Bedza60)

* If there is diagnostic uncertainty, consider:

* <u>Skin biopsy</u>: <u>Molluscum bodies</u> on <u>histopathology</u> confirm the diagnosis. [[1]](/library/8SdOYp0)[[2]](/library/Bedza60)

* <u>NAAT</u> testing (if available) [[2]](/library/Bedza60)

* Atypical or extensive spread: Consider evaluation for underlying immunocompromising conditions (e.g., <u>HIV testing</u>).

* <u>Genital lesions</u> in sexually active patients: <u>Screen for other STIs</u> (see “<u>STI screening</u>”). [[2]](/library/Bedza60)





> [!TIP]
> <u>Genital lesions</u> in children are usually caused by <u>autoinoculation</u> and do not necessarily indicate <u>sexual abuse</u>. [[1]](/library/8SdOYp0)[[2]](/library/Bedza60)

---

## Pathology

### <u>Histology</u> [[5]](/library/j-b_Cw)




* Localized to the <u>epidermis</u>

* H&E-stained sections demonstrate the following

* <u>Acanthosis</u> (thickened <u>epidermis</u>)

* Cup-shaped invagination (the <u>epidermis</u> invaginates into the <u>dermis</u>)

* Molluscum bodies: <u>keratinocytes</u> with eosinophilic intracytoplasmic <u>inclusion bodies</u> containing viral particles

## Treatment

### General principles [[1]](/library/8SdOYp0)[[2]](/library/Bedza60)




* <u>Expectant management</u> is usually sufficient for immunocompetent children.

* Advise patients and caregivers that lesions typically resolve spontaneously within 1 year. [[2]](/library/Bedza60)[[4]](/library/73d4Pp0)

* Recommend <u>infection control</u> measures.

* Indications for treatment of molluscum contagiosum lesions include: [[1]](/library/8SdOYp0)[[2]](/library/Bedza60)

* Extensive spread (e.g., in <u>immunocompromised individuals</u>)

* Complications (e.g., secondary bacterial infection)

* <u>Infection control</u> (e.g., sexually active individuals with <u>genital lesions</u>)

* Symptomatic control (e.g., <u>pruritus</u>)

* Cosmesis

* Treat underlying and associated conditions as indicated, e.g.,

* <u>Management of atopic dermatitis</u> and symptomatic <u>molluscum dermatitis</u>  [[6]](/library/j40_QT)[[7]](/library/hjdcZJ0)

* Optimization of <u>antiretroviral therapy</u> in patients with <u>HIV</u> [[4]](/library/73d4Pp0)[[8]](/library/u3dp4p0)





### <u>Infection control</u> measures [[1]](/library/8SdOYp0)[[2]](/library/Bedza60)




Measures that can reduce the possibility of spread to others include avoidance of:




* Scratching, shaving over, or picking at lesions

* Sharing towels or bed linen

* <u>Skin</u>-to-<u>skin</u> contact (cover lesions during contact sports and swimming)





> [!TIP]
> <u>Isolation precautions</u> are not indicated for patients with molluscum contagiosum as the risk of transmission is usually low. Children may attend school or daycare and participate in sports. [[2]](/library/Bedza60)




### Initial treatment options [[1]](/library/8SdOYp0)[[9]](/library/rXdfzo0)




* There is no consensus on molluscum contagiosum treatment.

* Educate patients that most treatment options cause <u>pain</u>, scarring, <u>blistering</u>, and pigment changes.





> [!TIP]
> <u>Cryotherapy</u>, <u>curettage</u>, and topical <u>cantharidin</u> are typically the most effective treatment options but require multiple sessions and should be administered by a healthcare professional. [[1]](/library/8SdOYp0)[[9]](/library/rXdfzo0)




#### Physical destruction




Physical destruction often requires <u>local anesthesia</u>, especially in young children.




* <u>Cryotherapy</u>

* <u>Curettage</u>

* <u>Electrodesiccation</u>

* Laser





#### Topical agents for chemical destruction




* Topical <u>cantharidin</u> DOSAGE (in individuals ≥ 2 years of age) [[1]](/library/8SdOYp0)[[2]](/library/Bedza60)

* <u>Berdazimer gel</u> DOSAGE (in individuals ≥ 1 year of age) [[10]](/library/whdhTp0)

* Other agents: <u>podophyllin</u>, <u>tretinoin</u>, <u>trichloroacetic acid</u>, <u>potassium</u> hydroxide  [[1]](/library/8SdOYp0)[[2]](/library/Bedza60)





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Cantharidin</u> should be applied by a trained healthcare professional due to the risk of adjacent tissue damage if incorrectly applied.




### Treatment of severe or refractory disease [[1]](/library/8SdOYp0)[[2]](/library/Bedza60)




* Refer to dermatology.

* <u>Cidofovir</u> may be considered in <u>immunocompromised individuals</u> with severe or refractory lesions.





> [!WARNING]
> The <u>antiviral agent</u> <u>cidofovir</u> should be reserved for severe disease (e.g., in <u>immunocompromised</u> patients) due to its adverse risk profile. [[2]](/library/Bedza60)
